“In the Year 2000…” sang *Late Night with Conan O’Brien* band member Richie “LaBamba” Rosenberg in a falsetto during one of the better-known skits of the 1990s. Conan and sidekick Andy Richter would then humorously imagine what the year 2000 would be like, including that “magic markers will smell worse” and presidential campaigns running ads “accusing their opponent of coming up with the idea for Jar Jar Binks.”

Turns out that the actual year 2000, being the last year before the world irrevocably changed after 9/11, and a year when [hardly any computer systems crashed](https://americanhistory.si.edu/collections/object-groups/y2k) due to a whole lot of hard work, was a year in which there were a metric ton of good movies.

Knowing what we know now, this list of the 100 Best Movies of 2000 is a starting point for numerous huge franchises, and a coming-out year for many of our favorite actors, actresses, and directors. Most especially, it’s the year when the world transitioned from VHS video tape into DVD, greatly enhancing resolution, sound, and the uncanny ability to find any scene you wanted.

Movies moved from something you *bought* or *rented* into something you *collected*. Built-in commentaries provided the layperson with crucial insight into the filmmaking process. Deleted scenes gave the fans glimpses into what got left on the cutting-room floor. For the first time, people started to understand that “widescreen” meant black bars on the top and bottom of your picture tube until TV dimensions caught up with the size and shape of movie theater screens.

Our criteria for this Top 100 of 2000 is threefold. First, Certified Fresh movies sorted by Tomatometer (***[Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/crouching_tiger_hidden_dragon)***, ***[Memento](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/memento)***, ***[Gladiator](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/gladiator)***). That’s followed by Fresh movies on with 40 or more critic reviews and 60% or higher on the Popcornmeter (***[Snatch](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/snatch)***, ***[Remember the Titans](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/remember_the_titans)***, ***[Unbreakable](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/unbreakable)***). And, finally, there’s Rotten movies with those same stats, with this last group considered cult classics and audience favorites (***[Miss Congeniality](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/miss_congeniality)***, ***[The Way of the Gun](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/way_of_the_gun)***, ***[Pitch Black](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/pitch_black)***).

The 73rd Academy Awards, broadcast March 25, 2001, honored movies released in theaters during the 2000 calendar year. Unlike the hesitant and hand-wringing 2002 broadcast, just a few months after 9/11 and featuring Tom Cruise giving a speech about how it’s still OK to like movies, this early 2001 event was full of optimism and verve. Steve Martin hosted for the first of three times.

In an extraordinary and unusual event, [Steven Sodberbergh](https://editorial.rottentomatoes.com/guide/steven-soderbergh-movies-shows/) competed against himself for Best Picture, clearly at the top of his game and nominated for two very different films: drug-trade thriller [***Traffic***](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/1103281-traffic) and earnest real-life legal drama [***Erin Brockovich***](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/erin_brockovich). The other Best Picture nominees were ***[Chocolat](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/chocolat)***, a film that combined sweets and sensuality to a delicious degree; Hong Kong martial-arts wuxia blockbuster *Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon* (and many viewers’ first experience with Chow-Yun Fat, Michelle Yeoh and director Ang Lee), and Best Picture winner *Gladiator*, one of five statues that Ridley Scott’s epic historical film would take home that night.

Snubbed from Best Picture were movies like the love letter to 1970s rock-n-roll and Rolling Stone ***[Almost Famous](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/almost_famous)***, [Christopher Nolan](https://editorial.rottentomatoes.com/guide/all-christopher-nolan-movies-ranked-by-tomatometer/)’s mind-bending *Memento*, the crowd-pleasing Tom Hanks desert island film [***Cast Away***](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/cast_away), and the downbeat psychological trip ***[Requiem for a Dream](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/requiem_for_a_dream)*.**

This one’s an honorable mention, falling just outside this top 100.

Other franchise starters include ***[X-Men](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/xmen)***, 20th Century Fox’s ambitious kick-in-the-pants to the Marvel movie revolution. Many *X*-sequels and spinoffs followed before Disney’s acquisition of Fox slowly integrated the mutants into the [Marvel Cinematic Universe](https://editorial.rottentomatoes.com/guide/marvel-movies-in-order/), beginning with 2024’s *[Deadpool vs. Wolverine](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/deadpool_and_wolverine)* and continuing with 2026’s *[Avengers: Doomsday](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/avengers_doomsday)*, which includes dozens of Marvel characters from every universe.

Box office titans ***[Meet the Parents](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/meet_the_parents)***, *Unbreakable*, *Chicken Run*, ***[Final Destination](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/final_destination)***, and honorable mentions ***[Charlie’s Angels](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/charlies_angels)*** and *Scary Movie* would kick off one or more sequels in succeeding years. Even *Pitch Black*, which only made $53 million worldwide, became a cult classic, introduced the world to Vin Diesel, and launched a series of Diesel pet projects and video games set in the same universe.

General audiences were not yet ready for more mature animated features, so Don Bluth’s space opera ***[Titan A.E.](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/titan_ae)*** landed with a thud initially, but became a cult classic later in life. Similarly, ***[The Road to El Dorado](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/road_to_el_dorado)***, the love triangle ode to Bob Hope’s road pictures that tried very hard to emulate a Disney movie, complete with Elton John soundtrack, may not have resonated with audiences at first, but found its way on home video.

One surprise misstep from Disney did not make this list, despite doing well at the box office: ***[Dinosaur](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/1097046-dinosaur)***,  an early CGI talking dinosaur picture not to be confused with [Pixar](https://editorial.rottentomatoes.com/guide/all-pixar-movies-ranked/)’s *[The Good Dinosaur](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/the_good_dinosaur)*.

Easily one of the most visually mesmerizing and heartbreakingly disturbing movies I've ever seen. It's a brutal movie about drug addiction. Yet the hypnotic cinematography and unorthodox editing of onscreen bodily sensations are very ethereal and suck you into its world. It's fun in the first half and slowly spirals into chaos and despair in the second half. Disturbing, yet fascinating. All thanks to the fantastic direction from Darren Aronofsky. The soundtrack is captivating, especially the titular music track Requiem for a Dream/Lux Aeterna. The cast is fantastic. The standout performance is from Ellen Burstyn, who acts her heart out into such a believable and heartbreaking character. The movie has great editing and stylized cinematography. You just want everyone to be happy, despite knowing the inevitability. The final half hour is incredibly tense and disorienting. It's an incredibly powerful cautionary tale about drug addiction AND how we as a society treat drug addicts.
